claim: Study 1 enrolled 40 healthy participants (14 male, mean age 26.1, range 22–31) in a behavioral-only risky-choice experiment, and Study 2 enrolled 44 healthy participants (19 male, mean age 30.6, range 23–50) in an fMRI version of the same experiment; the fMRI sample was reduced to 40 after excluding 4 participants for excessive head motion (>3 mm or >3°).
evidence: Forty healthy participants (14 male, mean age 26.1, range 22–31) participated in Study 1 (behaviour only study), and 44 healthy participants (19 male, mean (SD) age = 30.6 (6.5), range 23–50) participated in Study 2 (fMRI study). The fMRI data from four participants in Study 2 were excluded from the fMRI data analysis because of excessive head motion (>3 mm or >3°).

claim: The Study 2 sample size of 44 was determined prospectively by a power analysis (G*Power 3.1) targeting 95% power at alpha = 0.05 for a within-participant paired t-test, based on the guilt effect size of Cohen's d = 0.56 observed in Study 1.
evidence: The number of participants recruited in Study 2 corresponds to the sample size estimated using G*Power 3.1 software (Faul et al., 2007) for a two-way t-test assessing the difference between two means (matched pairs) based on the results of Study 1 (Cohen's d = 0.56), with alpha error = 0.05 and power (1 − beta) = 0.95, the required sample size was 44.

claim: In Study 2, the ostensible game partner was an experimenter (author MG or TW, matched by participant sex) located outside the scanner, not a fellow participant as in Study 1, representing a difference in the true social context between the two studies.
evidence: In Study 2, instead of playing against another same-sex participant, participants played either against experimenter MG or TW depending on sex (participant and partner were always of same sex) who were outside the scanner.
notes: In Study 1, partner was a real co-participant; in Study 2, the partner was an experimenter. Choices were simulated in both studies.

claim: The experiment partner's decisions were not made by a real person but were generated by a deterministic algorithm that always selected the option with the highest expected value (lottery chosen when EVdiff > 0), ensuring constant and predictable partner choices across participants.
evidence: In order to ascertain constant decisions by the partner, the partner's decisions were simulated using a simple algorithm that always selected the option with the highest expected value; i.e., it selected the lottery if EV diff > 0.
notes: This is a load-bearing assumption: the guilt manipulation depends on participants believing they affected a real partner, yet partner choices were deterministic. The methods do not state whether participants were informed of this.

claim: Participants' post-task ratings of their experiment partner on sympathy, cooperativity, honesty, openness, and sociability averaged above 8 on a 1–10 scale in both studies, validating that the icebreaker successfully established a positive and non-competitive social relationship.
evidence: Results of a brief questionnaire indicate that this approach was successful: participants' average ratings of their partners in terms of sympathy, cooperativity, honesty, openness and sociability were all above 8 on a scale of 1–10, in both studies (Appendix 1—table 11).

claim: Momentary happiness ratings were Z-scored per participant prior to all analyses to remove between-participant differences in rating variability, with no constant term included in computational models because Z-scoring sets each participant's mean rating to zero.
evidence: For analysis, happiness ratings were Z-scored to cancel out effects of different rating variabilities across participants. No constant term was used as ratings were Z-scored, resulting in a mean of the data of 0.

claim: Five nested computational models of momentary happiness (Basic, Inequality, Guilt-envy, Responsibility, and Responsibility Redux) were compared using AIC, BIC, R², adjusted R², and likelihood ratio tests to identify the best-fitting account of how outcomes and social responsibility modulate wellbeing.
evidence: To formally assess which of our models fitted the data best, we supplemented the AIC, BIC, R² and adjusted R² values reported in Table 1 with a series of likelihood ratio tests: we compared pair-wise the likelihoods of the Responsibility model given the data to the likelihoods of all the other models.
notes: The winning Responsibility Redux model (Equation 8) omits partner_pRPE from partner-choice trials but retains social_pRPE from participant-choice trials; its parameter estimates feed GLM2 for fMRI analysis.

claim: Parameter recovery simulations confirm that the computational happiness model parameters can be reliably recovered from synthetic data generated with each participant's fitted parameters plus 1 SD of added noise, across 10 repetitions per participant.
evidence: Stability of the estimated parameters of these models was evaluated by attempting to recover parameters from synthetic data created using each participant's real estimated parameters... The results show that the estimated parameters could be reliably recovered from noisy synthetic data.

claim: The mixed-effects regression of happiness after lottery outcomes including all three two-way interaction terms (participantHigh×partnerHigh, partnerHigh×participantDecided, participantHigh×participantDecided) fits the data significantly better than models without interactions (p < 2e−5) and not significantly worse than the full model with all interactions (p > 0.5) in both studies.
evidence: In both studies, the model reported in Equation 10 fitted the data significantly better (p < 2e−5) than the simpler models without interactions (higher total and adjusted R², see Appendix 1—table 2), but not significantly worse than the model with all interactions (p > 0.5; tested with the ANOVA function in R).
notes: This model selection justifies using the partnerHigh:participantDecided coefficient as the primary happiness-based measure of interpersonal guilt.

claim: All fMRI cluster activations reported survive family-wise error correction at p < 0.05 across the whole brain (or a specified smaller volume), based on an uncorrected voxel-forming threshold of p < 0.001.
evidence: All clusters reported survive a significance threshold of p < 0.05 with family-wise error correction for multiple comparisons across the whole brain or a smaller volume when explicitly mentioned, based on an uncorrected voxel-wise (cluster-forming) threshold of p < 0.001.
